prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are a new state of matter in which band topology and spin-orbit coupling give protected edge and surface states. The idea is clean, the theory is quantitative, and the predictions can be computed from first principles and compared with transport and photoemission. Kane and Mele supplied the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal. Molenkamp's group then observed the edge conduction in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, so the arc runs from theory through experiment, which is the pattern I trust. More than fifteen years of independent confirmation across HgTe, Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3-class materials, in transport and ARPES, make the interpretation stable. Band topology also changed how materials are classified and how they are searched for computationally. Four of eight members placed it in their top three, so it is not only my own field bias.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is credit. The three-name limit excludes Hasan, who led the first 3D observation, and it leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (deceased), whose HgTe proposal made Molenkamp's experiment possible, as well as Moore, Balents, Roy and Fu on the 3D theory. A prize framed as 2D quantum spin Hall can look arbitrary against the 3D story. The original Kane-Mele phase is also not realised in real graphene, because the spin-orbit gap is too small, so the theory's priority rests on the concept rather than the material. Applications remain modest. Finally, the 2016 prize already covered topological phases, and the optical lattice clock has far broader opening support than I can claim, so my own first place may reflect my specialism.

responses.point: Olsson ranks topological insulators second but proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, so that the prize pairs the theory with both the 2D (HgTe) and the 3D (ARPES) experimental discoveries and drops Mele.
responses.response: I take the point that 3D topological insulators are where the field became a materials-science programme, and Hasan's ARPES work is the kind of spectroscopic confirmation I value. But dropping Mele removes half of the original Z2 theory, and I find that harder to defend than leaving out an experimentalist, since Kane and Mele's two papers are the conceptual origin of both the 2D and the 3D cases. Keeping Hasan means the 3D theorists (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore, Balents; Roy) and the BHZ proposal also have a stronger claim for inclusion, and the priority between the Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 results is contested. I would prefer a prize built on the quantum spin Hall effect, where the chain from prediction to observation is cleanest. I would accept Hasan in place of Molenkamp only if the committee decides that the 3D discovery is the real unit.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks it second behind baryon acoustic oscillations. He notes that credit for the 3D case and for the BHZ prediction is contentious, that the 2016 topological-phase prize creates overlap, and that the committee may want to split spin Hall from 3D insulators.
responses.response: I agree on the credit problems, and I do not think a three-person prize can resolve them fully. On overlap, I disagree that 2016 is a serious obstacle. That prize honoured topological phase transitions and the Kosterlitz-Thouless-type physics and Haldane's work on the Hall insulator and chain. Z2 topological insulators with protected helical edge states are a different discovery and a separate experimental programme. I am less able to judge baryon acoustic oscillations, which is far from my field. I accept that it is a clean, reproduced result, but I would want to hear whether the committee is comfortable with a cosmology prize after 2006, 2011 and 2019. Splitting 2D from 3D into two prize parts would cost us a coherent citation, and the name limit would leave at most one or two people per part.

responses.point: Lindroth gives optical lattice clocks first place. She values independent laboratories agreeing at the 1e-18 level, and she regards the lattice clock as a distinct step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I find this the strongest competing case, and I share her weighting of independent agreement between laboratories. The clock result is as reproducible as anything on our list, and the Katori and Ye attribution is much cleaner than mine. My doubt is whether it is a discovery or a precision instrument, and Danielsson and Pearce both flag the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion prize. I would not oppose it. If the committee finds the topological credit unresolvable, then B022 is my first alternative, and I would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested three-name list.

responses.point: Mehlig supports the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio, and sees the theory and the HgTe observation as the decisive steps. He also notes that the 3D credit stays unresolved, with Zhang unable to be recognised.
responses.response: I agree with the trio and with the unresolved 3D credit. Zhang's death means the BHZ proposal cannot be honoured by name, and I think the citation should be worded around the quantum spin Hall effect and its observation so it does not claim more than the three laureates did. I would also say that this is a recollection-based reading of the credit history, and I would like the committee's documentation to check it before we decide.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers the theory-led trio over a configuration including Hasan and the 3D experiments, and whether 2D and 3D topological insulators should be treated as one achievement.
Whether the optical lattice clock, which has the broadest opening support, should take precedence over a topological prize with contested attribution.
My recollection of the credit history (Kane-Mele, BHZ, Konig et al., Hasan) is from memory and has not been checked against the documentation.
Whether the pairing mechanism debate and twist-angle disorder make magic-angle graphene (B030) too early, as I currently judge, or whether a few more years would change that view.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I work in theoretical condensed-matter physics and electronic-structure theory in the same broad area as topological band theory, and I have no known personal, institutional or collaborative tie to any credited name on the shortlist. My field bias should be discounted accordingly.
